newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels defiant, dash hopes of quick solution.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels defiant, dash hopes of quick solution.

text.p: Marxist guerrillas holding more than 80 hostages in the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima vowed defiance on Tuesday, saying they were ready for the "ultimate sacrifice" and would not relax their demands.

Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini said the rebels, who have held the residence for two weeks, were not prepared to go back on their demand for the release of about 400 jailed comrades.

"We are inflexible in our original position, Cerpa said in a brief walkie-talkie interview with Reuters. He dashed speculation that the siege was close to an end, telling reporters allowed into the residence for the first time: "I do not see an immediate solution"
He said he was "open to any mediator ... (Cuban leader Fidel) Castro or (Russian President) Boris Yeltsin or whoever."
The rebels' key hostage, Peruvian Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela, also speaking to reporters inside the residence, called for a peaceful solution.
Earlier, President Alberto Fujimori and Prime Minister Alberto Pandolfi had both expressed confidence that the crisis would be brought to a peaceful end.
Cerpa told Reuters the MRTA had already achieved its aim of drawing world attention to the bad conditions of Peruvian jails, and would concentrate on obtaining the release of prisoners.

He said responsibility for resolving the crisis lay with the government. "There has been no opening up. This is now in the hands of the government. The government must reflect. This is not in our hands," Cerpa said.
A group of about a dozen cameramen and photographers was allowed inside the building for the first time to see the conditions in which 83 hostages are being held by about 20 heavily-armed rebels.
The journalists met Cerpa and about four other rebels wearing combat gear with ammunition strapped to their bodies.

Reuters photographer Zoraida Diaz, among the journalists who entered the building, said the rebels spoke calmly, insisted they were not terrorists and repeated demands for improved jail conditions for their comrades.
Diaz said furniture was pushed up against windows inside the building. "Any object you can see has been pushed against the walls or put up against the windows," she said.
Hostages were seen waving at journalists from the residence windows. Tudela looked relaxed and in good spirits.
The Red Cross, apparently unhappy that journalists were allowed into the mined and booby-trapped compound, said it had withdrawn "temporarily" from the site.
The sudden activity on Tuesday followed rising hopes that the crisis was about to end.

The defiant tone of rebel statements contrasted with a more conciliatory mood since the weekend release of 20 hostages and a first face-to-face meeting between the guerrillas and government negotiator Domingo Palermo. He visited for a second time late on Monday.

An unidentified rebel inside the building slammed Fujimori's government as a "dictatorship" that did not care about poverty. He shouted that the guerrillas were "determined to make the ultimate sacrifice."
"Peru is not a democracy. It is a dictatorship dressed up as a democracy," he said from behind a window. "There is state terrorism that kills through starvation."
He added: "Any harm to them (the remaining hostages) will be the exclusive responsibility of the government of Mr Fujimori if he decides upon a military intervention."

In an interview with the Spanish news agency Efe made available to Reuters, Fujimori said earlier on Tuesday the crisis could be resolved without violence but insisted the guerrillas lay down their arms and free all their captives.
"I believe that in the end reason will impose a solution without the spilling of blood, fully respectful of the human rights of the hostages and hostage-takers," he said.

Fujimori said he would not free any MRTA members from Peru's prisons. He said that if his government was to rule out the use of force, the rebels must put down their weapons and free the hostages to a "commission of guarantors".
Police allowed journalists to approach the building in small groups from around 10.30 a.m. (1530 GMT). One group went into the building at about 11 a.m. (1600 GMT).

In Tokyo, Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said he was confident of the Peruvian government's ability to handle the crisis -- so much so that he was going ahead with a five- nation Asian trip next week that officials had earlier said might be cancelled.

Hashimoto said he did not think the crisis would necessarily be over by the time he starts his trip on Jan. 7, but added that slow progress was a sign that Peruvian authorities were working for a peaceful solution.
The remaining hostages included three ambassadors, dozens of Japanese businessmen and most of the top brass of Peru's police and intelligence forces.
